bull_thesis:
The bull case starts with a correction, not a forecast. Our screener shows Genmab's revenue down 82% and earnings per share down 87% year over year. Neither happened. Genmab changed its reporting currency from Danish kroner to US dollars with the 2025 accounts: 2024 was reported as DKK 21.53 billion of revenue, 2025 as $3.86 billion. Translated at roughly 6.9 kroner to the dollar, 2024 revenue was about $3.12 billion, so 2025 revenue actually grew about a fifth - exactly what management claimed on the 17 February 2026 call. The apparent collapse is a units mismatch. What is underneath is a business compounding at a rate few large-cap biotechnology companies manage.

The operating record supports that. First-half 2026 revenue of $2.05 billion was up about 23% on the same period of 2025, and on 6 August 2026 management raised full-year guidance to $4.3-4.5 billion - 19% growth at the midpoint against the 14% previously guided - while raising operating-profit guidance 7% and letting operating expenses rise only 2%. Raising the revenue line and cutting the growth rate of spending in the same breath, in a quarter when you also announce two brand-new Phase 3 trials, is genuine operating leverage rather than a presentation choice.

The revenue base is also getting less concentrated, which is the structural worry on this name. The chief financial officer's most useful sentence on 6 August 2026: 'approximately half of our year over year revenue growth came from DARZALEX. Impressively, the other half generated by EPKINLY and the remainder of our portfolio.' DARZALEX (daratumumab, the multiple-myeloma antibody Genmab licensed to Johnson & Johnson) still supplies roughly half of revenue as a near-costless royalty - J&J reported $4.21 billion of DARZALEX net sales in the second quarter of 2026 alone, disclosed 15 July 2026. But EPKINLY (epcoritamab, a lymphoma antibody) grew 48% in the first half to $312 million, TIVDAK (for cervical cancer) grew 18%, and the rest of the royalty book grew 35%.

EPKINLY's growth is not a launch curve running on inertia; specific barriers are being removed. In March 2026 the US Food and Drug Administration removed the recommendation for 24-hour hospitalisation after the first full dose in later-line diffuse large B-cell lymphoma - the single biggest obstacle to using the drug in community practices, where most patients are actually treated. On 6 July 2026 the European Commission approved the chemotherapy-free EPKINLY-plus-lenalidomide-and-rituximab combination in second-line follicular lymphoma, the first bispecific-based regimen approved in Europe in that setting. On 29 June 2026 the Phase 3 EPCORE DLBCL-4 trial met its primary endpoint on progression-free survival. Management now says over 90% of key customers order for two or more sites.

Then there is the option value the market is arguably not paying for. Genmab has three late-stage owned assets and, as of 6 August 2026, dates for all of them. Rina-S (rinatabart sesutecan, an antibody-drug conjugate targeting folate receptor alpha) reads out in both Phase 2 and Phase 3 in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer in the fourth quarter of 2026 - pulled forward because enrollment finished ahead of plan, disclosed 14 May 2026. It has a breakthrough therapy designation in endometrial cancer, a 55.6% confirmed response rate in heavily pretreated ovarian patients regardless of folate-receptor expression, and no ocular toxicity, lung inflammation or nerve damage seen across the programme - the three toxicities that limit the incumbent drug in this class. Petosemtamab, the asset Genmab bought Merus for, reads out in frontline head-and-neck cancer in the fourth quarter; its Phase 2 combination with pembrolizumab produced a 63% response rate against roughly 19% for standard of care, and it carries two breakthrough designations. EPKINLY's frontline lymphoma interim analysis - the largest patient population in the whole portfolio, roughly 70,000 people - also lands in the fourth quarter.

Management has earned the right to be believed on dates. Over six quarters they promised a decision on GEN1042 and killed it on time (November 2025); promised three Rina-S Phase 3 trials by year-end 2025 and delivered them; promised focused acquisitions and did the Merus deal; and pulled the ovarian readout forward rather than pushing it back. Our screener records a five-of-seven quarterly earnings-beat rate.

For the bull case to pay, three things must hold. First, DARZALEX must keep compounding into the end of the decade - it grew 21% in the first half of 2026 and consensus estimates on file model group revenue rising to $6.57 billion by 2030 with no erosion inside the window. Second, at least two of the four fourth-quarter readouts must succeed, converting roughly $9.8 billion of acquisition spending from an intangible asset into approved products with 2027 launches. Third, leverage must come down as promised - the chief financial officer committed on 17 February 2026 to below three times gross leverage by the end of 2027, from 3.8 times today. If all three hold, this is a company earning consensus $25.55 per share in 2028 against a Copenhagen price of DKK 2,124, or about $332 - thirteen times.
bear_thesis:
The bear case does not need Genmab to be a bad business. It needs only two things to be true at once: that the price already reflects the good outcome, and that the company has removed its own margin for error.

Start with what changed on the balance sheet. Through mid-2025 Genmab was a self-funding royalty annuity - 'we ended the first half with around $3 billion in cash,' management said on 7 August 2025, 'reinforcing the strength of our financial foundation.' Then it borrowed $5.5 billion at a weighted-average effective rate of about 6.6% to buy Merus for roughly $7.5 billion of cash. At 30 June 2026 the company holds $1.50 billion of cash against $5.27 billion of debt - net debt of $3.77 billion including $138 million of capitalised leases, or about $3.63 billion on the ex-lease basis filings usually quote. Interest expense went from $9 million in the second quarter of 2025 to $110 million in the second quarter of 2026. Roughly $440 million a year now sits ahead of the equity, permanently, whatever the trials do. The financial-strength language simply stopped appearing on the calls; it was never withdrawn.

Second, cash conversion has broken down and nobody has been asked about it. First-half 2026 cash from operations was $54 million against $114 million a year earlier - down 53% - on 23% higher revenue. Free cash flow over the trailing twelve months is $870 million against $1.39 billion of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation. The second quarter alone consumed $267 million of working capital as the royalty receivable owed by Johnson & Johnson built to $1.28 billion, or 48 days of sales. Reported profit growth is real; the cash behind it in 2026 is not showing up yet. Separately, the first-half effective tax rate was 3.6% - $13 million of tax on $348 million of pre-tax profit - from deferred tax assets recognised in the Merus integration, which management says will normalise over 12 to 18 months. Roughly $60-70 million of first-half earnings will not repeat.

Third, the asset base is now mostly promises. Goodwill and intangible assets stand at $9.23 billion, 73.7% of total assets. Tangible asset value is negative, about -$3.3 billion. Return on invested capital is 9.9% and return on equity 13.6% - respectable, but barely above a plausible cost of capital, and a long way from the returns this company earned as a pure royalty house. If petosemtamab fails in the fourth quarter, the write-down is mechanical and it is large, and it arrives on top of the clinical disappointment and the debt.

Fourth - and this is the specific risk, not a general one - four registrational readouts have been compressed into a single quarter with no staggering: Rina-S in ovarian cancer (both Phase 2 and Phase 3), petosemtamab in frontline head-and-neck, and EPKINLY's frontline lymphoma interim analysis, all in the fourth quarter of 2026. The one completed Phase 3 in this portfolio that has already reported shows exactly the failure mode to fear: EPCORE DLBCL-1 improved progression-free survival and missed on overall survival (announced January 2026), and it required a formal joint 'clarification on the primary endpoints' release with AbbVie on 23 July 2026, six months later. The chief medical officer's own explanation on 14 May 2026 - that showing a survival benefit 'is becoming a little bit more challenging in diffuse large B-cell in general because of the increasing availability of very effective salvage therapies' - is a structural argument, and structural arguments do not stop applying to the next trial. Frontline head-and-neck cancer, meanwhile, is a graveyard for drugs that looked excellent in single-arm Phase 2 work; a 63% response rate in a small combination cohort is encouraging, not predictive.

There is also an unasked question with more money attached than any of the above. Roughly half of revenue is a royalty on daratumumab, and daratumumab's exclusivity does not last forever. Across six earnings calls not one analyst asked about the loss-of-exclusivity horizon, biosimilar filings, or what the royalty looks like in the 2030s, and management never volunteered it. Consensus estimates on file carry revenue rising to $6.57 billion by 2030 with no erosion modelled anywhere in the window - while the 2028 earnings-per-share range runs from $16.20 to $34.36, a spread of more than double that quietly encodes the disagreement nobody voices. Every dollar of that royalty funds the research programme that is supposed to replace it. If the replacement is late, the arithmetic is unforgiving.

Finally, the entry price offers nothing for taking any of this. At DKK 2,124 the shares sit 86% up their 52-week range and about 15% above the 200-day average, at roughly 5.8 times enterprise value to revenue and 17.2 times enterprise value to EBITDA. There is no structural floor beneath the price - no deal terms, no net cash, no tender - because the balance sheet is net levered. What confirms the bear case: a miss on either petosemtamab or Rina-S in the fourth quarter; a repeat of the progression-free-survival-win, overall-survival-miss pattern in the frontline lymphoma interim; a second consecutive half of cash conversion below 50% of EBITDA; or any disclosure that shortens the daratumumab royalty runway.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is not the direction of the business - it is what the market is pricing and what our own data pipeline told us.

The first disagreement is with ourselves, and it has to be said first because it is the reason this name reached the committee. Genmab surfaced as a deep-value candidate on a claimed 73% margin of safety from the discounted-cash-flow model, 70% from owner earnings, and a headline -82% revenue decline that looked like a fear print. All of it is an artifact of a reporting-currency change from Danish kroner to US dollars in the 2025 accounts. There is no fear print here. The market never repriced Genmab for terminal decline; our measurement did. The honest read is that the shares trade at 5.8 times enterprise value to revenue, 17.2 times enterprise value to EBITDA and about 13.8 times the 2028 consensus earnings estimate, 86% up the 52-week range - a fair price for a good business, not a mispricing.

The second disagreement is with the street, and it is real. The published consensus estimates carry Genmab revenue rising from $4.38 billion in 2026 to $6.57 billion in 2030 with no daratumumab erosion modelled anywhere inside the forecast window. Roughly half of revenue is a royalty on daratumumab, and a royalty has a statutory end. The spread inside the estimates gives the game away: the 2028 earnings-per-share range runs from $16.20 to $34.36, more than a factor of two, on 15 contributing analysts. That is not disagreement about a product launch; that is unvoiced disagreement about the royalty runway. Across all six earnings calls in our transcript set, not one analyst asked about loss of exclusivity, biosimilar filings, or the royalty's end date, and management never volunteered it. When the whole sell side declines to ask the question that drives half the revenue, the consensus number is a placeholder rather than a forecast.

The third disagreement runs in Genmab's favour and is the reason this is a watchlist rather than a pass. The market is treating this as a single-bet story - buy the Merus deal, hope petosemtamab works. The disclosure that contradicts that came on 6 August 2026: 'approximately half of our year over year revenue growth came from DARZALEX. Impressively, the other half generated by EPKINLY and the remainder of our portfolio.' EPKINLY grew 48% in the first half, the rest of the royalty book grew 35%, and guidance was raised from 14% to 19% growth while spending guidance rose only 2%. The base is broadening while the market watches the pipeline. That is the thing worth owning - at a price that reflects it.

The fourth disagreement is one nobody on either side has priced. First-half 2026 cash from operations was $54 million against $114 million a year earlier - down 53% on 23% higher revenue - and trailing free cash flow of $870 million against $1.39 billion of EBITDA. Some of that is a working-capital build in the Johnson & Johnson royalty receivable and should reverse; some of it is $440 million a year of new interest that will not. Neither management nor a single analyst mentioned it on the 6 August call. In a tape that has spent this year re-pricing companies on funding quality rather than revenue - the memory names bought because cash flow covers capital spending, the capital-spending payers sold - an unremarked halving of operating cash flow is the kind of detail that gets discovered at an inconvenient moment.

positioning_washout:
There is no forced-selling mechanism here, and pretending otherwise would be the wrong analysis. Genmab pays no dividend and never has, so there is no yield-focused shareholder base to be flushed by a cut. There is no pivot, no restructuring, no index migration pending, and no credit event in view. The shares trade in two liquid venues - Copenhagen as the primary listing and a Nasdaq depositary receipt at one-tenth of the Copenhagen share - so index and passive flow is stable in both.

What the shareholder register does show is the opposite of forced selling. If the fourth-quarter data disappoints, that money leaves in days, into a register whose natural long-term holders are already sized. The shares sit 86% up their 52-week range and roughly 15% above the 200-day average, having run from a DKK 1,512 low - so the marginal holder today is closer to their entry than to their conviction. What stops it being a buy today is the shape of the risk, not the quality of the company. Genmab has converted itself from a self-funding royalty annuity into a levered, binary bet: $3.77 billion of net debt where there was $3 billion of cash eighteen months ago, roughly $440 million a year of interest permanently ahead of the equity, $9.23 billion of intangible assets against negative tangible book value - and four registrational readouts compressed into a single quarter. The one completed Phase 3 that has reported showed exactly the pattern to fear: a progression-free-survival win and an overall-survival miss, requiring a formal clarification with AbbVie six months later. And first-half operating cash flow halved to $54 million on 23% higher revenue, a fact neither management nor a single analyst mentioned. In a tape that has spent this year separating companies whose cash flow covers their spending from those whose does not, that gap deserves an explanation before capital, not after.

On our reconciled parts - the royalty book at roughly $13.8 billion, own commercial products at $6.3 billion, risk-adjusted pipeline at $5.3 billion, less $3.77 billion of net debt - fair value is about DKK 2,250 against a DKK 2,124 last trade. One genuine credit the regime does earn this name: nothing about an ovarian-cancer or lymphoma readout depends on oil, artificial-intelligence capital spending, or the Federal Reserve, and in a tape where most theses have collapsed onto two or three shared factors, that independence is worth something. ---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Genmab spent these six quarters executing one consistent story, and unusually for a biotechnology company, it did not move the goalposts.

The story opens in May 2025 as a **transition narrative**: a royalty-funded antibody house becoming "a fully integrated biotech independently developing and commercializing wholly owned antibody differentiated therapies." At that point the company had two marketed medicines it partly owned — EPKINLY (epcoritamab, a lymphoma antibody partnered with AbbVie) and TIVDAK (tisotumab vedotin, for cervical cancer) — plus one late-stage owned asset, Rina-S (rinatabart sesutecan, an antibody-drug conjugate for ovarian and endometrial cancer). Management framed 2025 around three commitments repeated verbatim on every call since: accelerate the late-stage pipeline, maximise the commercialised medicines, stay disciplined on capital.

Three things then **expanded** the story:

- **Rina-S went from one Phase 3 trial to five programmes.** In May 2025 there was one Phase 3 in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer. By February 2026 there were three (adding endometrial and platinum-sensitive ovarian), plus signal-seeking Phase 2 work in lung and, by 2026, gastrointestinal cancers.
- **The company bought its third pillar.** In November 2025 Genmab announced the acquisition of Merus for petosemtamab ("peto"), an EGFR/LGR5 bispecific antibody in head-and-neck cancer, closing in early Q1 2026 for roughly $7.5 billion of cash. It was funded with a **$5.5 billion debt offering** — the first time in the company's history that leverage, rather than royalty cash, paid for growth.
- **Peto then expanded again.** On 2026-08-06 management added two new Phase 3 trials in colorectal cancer, on top of two ongoing head-and-neck Phase 3s and a planned locally-advanced head-and-neck study.

Two things were **quietly dropped**, and to management's credit, both were announced rather than allowed to fade:

- **GEN1042** (a CD40/4-1BB antibody with BioNTech) was under "duration data" review in May 2025 ("that decision will be taken in the second half of this year") and was formally killed on the November 2025 call: "the current data in frontline head and neck cancer for GEN1042 did not meet our high bar for continued development." A clean, on-schedule kill.
- **Acasunlimab** has been demoted without ever being formally shelved. It was named as one of the three or four "high-impact late-stage" programmes in mid-2025 and got a Phase 2 melanoma study; by the February 2026 "three programmes" slide it had been replaced by petosemtamab, and it goes unmentioned on the 2026 calls. That is a substitution, not a disclosure failure — but it is a substitution the company never narrated.

The arc as of today: **from a royalty annuity with a pipeline, to a levered three-asset oncology company whose value now hinges on four clinical readouts landing in a single quarter.** Management's own framing on 2026-08-06 was that the second half is "what we have been building towards."

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

### The headline that must be corrected before anything else

Our screener shows **revenue down 82.1% year over year, earnings per share down 86.9%, and free cash flow down 84.3%.** Those numbers are arithmetic on mixed units and describe nothing that happened to this business.

Genmab **changed its reporting currency from Danish kroner to US dollars with the 2025 fiscal year.** The 2024 accounts report revenue of DKK 21.53 billion; the 2025 accounts report revenue of $3.86 billion. Translating 2024 at roughly 6.9 kroner to the dollar gives about $3.12 billion, so the true 2025 move was revenue **up roughly a fifth**, which is exactly what management claimed on the February 2026 call ("in 2025, we grew total revenue by 19%"). The same applies to earnings per share: DKK 121.36 in 2024 is about $17.6, against $15.94 reported for 2025 — a mid-single-digit to high-single-digit decline caused by higher research spending, not an 87% collapse.

This matters twice over. First, **every valuation model in our stack that was fed the raw series is wrong** — the discounted-cash-flow fair value of DKK 8,007 (a claimed 73% margin of safety) and the "owner earnings +70%" reading are outputs of a model that saw an 82% revenue collapse followed by an assumed recovery. Second, our own peer-comparison file reached the right conclusion — "that decline looks like a base effect... rather than a genuine operating collapse" — but for the **wrong reason**. It attributed the drop to lumpy royalty timing. It is a currency relabelling. The conclusion survives; the reasoning does not, and a reason that happens to be wrong is not evidence.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Reliability: High.**

| Phase 3 in endometrial cancer to start "before the end of the year" | May 2025 | Delivered; announced initiated November 2025 |

| Full-year 2026 revenue growth | Guided ~14% | **Raised to 19% at the midpoint** ($4.3–4.5B) on 2026-08-06, with operating profit guidance up 7% to $1.1–1.4B |

Our screener records a **five-of-seven quarterly earnings-beat rate (71%)**, which is consistent with this pattern: a team that guides to what it believes and modestly exceeds it, rather than one that sandbags hard. The mid-year guidance raise — revenue up 5%, operating profit up 7%, spending up only 2% — is the strongest single credibility datapoint in the file, because it is a *number* rather than a narrative, and it was raised in the same quarter they announced two expensive new trials.

**The offsetting mark.** The EPCORE DLBCL-1 overall-survival miss was announced in January 2026 and then required a formal **"clarification on the primary endpoints" release on 2026-07-23**, six months later, issued jointly with AbbVie. A company that has to re-explain the endpoints of a completed Phase 3 half a year after topline is a company whose first disclosure was not clear enough. That is one blemish on an otherwise clean sheet, and it belongs on the record.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**The recurring deflection: what hazard ratio would count as success.** Asked directly by Wolfe Research (Q1 2026) and repeatedly before, the answer is always a version of "it doesn't make much sense to speculate." Management substitutes the Phase 2 read-across ("Phase IIIs have in the past on EPKINLY tended to mimic close Phase II data") for a bar. That substitution is precisely what the DLBCL-1 monotherapy result already falsified once: strong Phase 2 data, a Phase 3 that hit progression-free survival and missed overall survival.

**The question that got a non-answer, and matters.** On 2026-08-06, Guggenheim's Michael Schmidt asked why the frontline lymphoma interim analysis is landing in Q4 2026 when his team's work suggested it should have occurred "at some point last year" — a roughly one-year delay in an event-driven trial that **enrolled faster than expected**. The reply did not address the question at all; it pivoted to how exciting the Phase 2 data are and closed with "we should probably leave it at this at this point." Slow event accrual in an oncology trial can mean the control arm is doing better than modelled. It can equally mean the treatment arm is doing very well. Management chose not to say which, and no one followed up.

**Timing shape.** Barclays (2026-08-06) asked the sharpest structural question in the whole set: if the interim analysis fails, will investors be told, or will silence be the signal? Two other analysts asked whether the ovarian Phase 2 and Phase 3 datasets will be released together or separately. Both go to the same worry — **the information flow around a four-readout quarter is not yet defined**, and disclosure ambiguity around binary events is where shareholders get hurt.

**What analysts are not asking, and should be.** Not one question across six calls addresses the durability of the DARZALEX royalty — the loss-of-exclusivity horizon for daratumumab, biosimilar filings, or what the royalty stream looks like in the 2030s. This is roughly half of company revenue and the asset that funds everything else. Consensus reflects the same blind spot: analyst estimates on file show revenue rising from $4.38B (2026) to $6.57B (2030) with **no cliff modelled anywhere inside the forecast window** — while the 2028 estimate range runs from $16.20 to $34.36 in earnings per share, a spread of more than double that quietly encodes exactly the disagreement nobody voices.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The balance sheet changed character and the commentary did not.** "Over $3 billion in cash, reinforcing the strength of our financial foundation" (May 2025) became $1.50 billion of cash against $5.27 billion of debt by June 2026, and no call since has reframed the financial-strength language. Roughly $440 million a year of interest now sits ahead of the equity at a weighted-average effective rate of about 6.6% (CFO, February 2026).

🔴 **Cash conversion deteriorated while profit grew.** First-half 2026 operating cash flow of $54 million against $114 million a year earlier, on 23% higher revenue (Section 2). Unremarked by management and unasked by analysts.

🔴 **Nearly three-quarters of total assets are intangible, and tangible book value is negative** (about −$3.3 billion). A petosemtamab failure produces a large, mechanical write-down on top of the clinical disappointment.

🔴 **Four registrational readouts compressed into one quarter.** Concentration in time is itself a risk: Q4 2026 carries Rina-S in ovarian cancer (Phase 2 and Phase 3), petosemtamab in frontline head-and-neck, and EPKINLY in frontline lymphoma. There is no staggering to absorb a bad print.

🔴 **The one endpoint miss on record is the one that repeats.** EPCORE DLBCL-1 won on progression-free survival and lost on overall survival (January 2026). The chief medical officer's own explanation on 2026-05-14 — that showing a survival benefit "is becoming a little bit more challenging in diffuse large B-cell in general because of the increasing availability of very effective salvage therapies" — is a structural argument, and structural arguments do not stop applying to the next trial.

🔴 **A programme was substituted out of the top tier without narration.** Acasunlimab went from a named late-stage priority (2025) to absent from the three-pillar slide (2026) with no discontinuation announcement.

🟢 **They killed a programme on schedule.** GEN1042 was flagged for a decision in May 2025 and discontinued in November 2025 for failing "our high bar." Most managements let weak assets drift.

🟢 **They pulled a readout forward.** Completing enrollment early in the platinum-resistant ovarian Phase 3 (2026-05-14) is verifiable operational execution, not a claim.

🟢 **They raised guidance and cut the growth rate of spending in the same breath** (2026-08-06): revenue guidance up 5%, operating profit up 7%, operating expenses up only 2% — while adding two new Phase 3 trials.

🟢 **Growth broadened away from the single royalty.** The CFO's most useful disclosure on 2026-08-06: "approximately half of our year over year revenue growth came from DARZALEX. Impressively, the other half generated by EPKINLY and the remainder of our portfolio." That is the concentration risk actively reducing, measurably.

🟢 **Commercial execution is real and independent of partners.** EPKINLY grew 48% in the first half of 2026, the label lost its 24-hour hospitalisation recommendation in March 2026 (a genuine barrier removal for community oncology), the European Commission approved the follicular-lymphoma combination on 2026-07-06, and Genmab launched TIVDAK on its own in Japan and Europe without a partner for the first time.

🟢 **A deep-value institution crossed the disclosure line.** Orbis Investment Management reported 4.99% of the share capital as of 2026-06-12 — the kind of holder that arrives when it believes the market is mispricing durable cash flow.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**"Multibillion dollar" is doing load-bearing work.** EPKINLY has a peak-sales number (over $3 billion). Rina-S has one ($2 billion-plus). Petosemtamab — the asset that cost $7.5 billion of cash and the entire balance sheet — has only "multibillion blockbuster potential," and when Handelsbanken asked in February 2026 what it would take to convert that into an actual figure, the CFO explicitly declined to say when he would say ("I'm not going to front run this"). A precise number for the cheap assets and a vague one for the expensive asset is a tell about internal confidence intervals.

**The vocabulary migrated from "partner" to "wholly owned."** In May 2025 the phrasing was aspirational: "becoming a fully integrated biotech." By November 2025 the acquisition "accelerates our shift towards a 100% owned model." The economics follow the words — owned assets carry the full cost and the full margin, which is why operating expenses now run near $2.9 billion against $4.4 billion of revenue.

**A quiet, unexplained tax anomaly.** The effective tax rate for the first half of 2026 was **3.6%** — $13 million of tax on $348 million of pre-tax profit — attributed to "recognition and utilization of deferred tax assets" from the Merus integration, with normalisation promised "over the next 12 to 18 months." Roughly $60–70 million of first-half earnings are therefore non-recurring. It was disclosed, which is to management's credit; it was not adjusted out of any headline, which is not.

**The safety differentiation is stated more insistently over time.** Every Rina-S discussion now carries the same clause: "no signals of ocular toxicity, interstitial lung disease or neuropathy across the entire program." That is a direct, unnamed comparison to the incumbent folate-receptor drug in this space. Repetition of a competitive claim that no regulator has yet adjudicated is worth noting.

**No management turnover.** The same four executives — van de Winkel, Pagano, Bailey, Ahmadi — present every call in the same order, with Klimovsky on questions. Continuity is a mild positive; it also means there is no fresh voice to contradict the house view.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT

**Classification: STRENGTHENING.**

The commercial base is compounding (revenue up roughly a quarter, EPKINLY up 48%, guidance raised mid-year), the promise-to-delivery record over six quarters is close to clean, and the revenue base is measurably broadening away from its single royalty. Management kills what fails, pulls forward what works, and gives dates it can be held to.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing a position:**

> Genmab has converted itself from a self-funding royalty annuity into a **levered, binary bet whose entire pipeline value resolves in one quarter.** Net debt of $3.77 billion, negative tangible book value, and $9.2 billion of intangible assets now sit against four registrational readouts landing in Q4 2026 and Q1 2027. The business quality is not in question; the *position* quality is entirely a question of price and timing. At DKK 2,124 — 86% up its 52-week range, 15% above its 200-day average, and near the top of the range — the market is not offering a discount for accepting that concentration. **Do not confuse the screener's 73% margin of safety for an opportunity: it is an artifact of feeding a currency relabelling into a growth model.**

**Economic moat: NARROW, and stable rather than eroding.**

The moat type is **intangible-asset and regulatory** — patented antibody sequences, the DuoBody bispecific platform, orphan and breakthrough designations, and manufacturing know-how. The evidence supports narrow rather than wide in both directions:

- *For a real moat:* gross margin of 91.7% and a royalty stream requiring almost no capital (capital expenditure is 0.24% of revenue) is a genuinely exceptional economic structure. Competitors cannot replicate a granted patent.
- *Against a wide moat:* return on invested capital is **9.9%**, barely above a reasonable cost of capital, and return on equity 13.6%. More fundamentally, **a moat with a statutory expiry date is not a wide one.** Every dollar of royalty revenue has a known end.
- The gross-margin "contraction" our screener flags is **mix, not pricing pressure** — pure royalty revenue at nearly 100% margin is being diluted by own-product sales that carry manufacturing cost. That is the strategy working, not the moat failing.
- The returns decline is the Merus purchase price entering the capital base, not competitive erosion. Hence **STABLE**, not eroding.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL — and it is not one of the catalogued structural forces.**

None of the standard secular tails apply here: no artificial-intelligence displacement, no payments disintermediation, no reimbursement compression of consequence. The terminal-value question is **idiosyncratic and contractual — the loss-of-exclusivity horizon on daratumumab (DARZALEX)**, which supplies roughly half of revenue and funds the entire research programme. Biosimilar competition to daratumumab is in development industry-wide, and the exact royalty-term end could not be established from the materials provided; it is not discussed on any of the six calls and is not modelled in consensus estimates through 2030. It is therefore material rather than terminal, for two reasons: the erosion is dated and gradual rather than a cliff into nothing, and Genmab is visibly and expensively replacing it — three owned late-stage assets, two acquisitions, $9.8 billion committed. Whether the replacement arrives before the erosion is **the** question on this name.

**Fear-print or value trap?** Neither, which is the awkward answer. The cheapness signal that surfaced this name is a **measurement artifact**, not a fear print — the market never repriced Genmab for terminal decline; our data pipeline mislabelled a currency change as one. On the honest numbers the shares trade at roughly 5.8x enterprise value to revenue, 17.2x enterprise value to EBITDA, and 13x the 2028 consensus earnings estimate. That is a fair price for a good business with a dated risk, not a mispricing.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory improving · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat material.

# Genmab A/S (GMAB.CO) — Forensic Dossier

**Prepared:** 7 September 2026 · **Listing used throughout:** Copenhagen ordinary shares, quoted in Danish kroner (DKK). Live quote DKK 2,143 (previous close DKK 2,165; 52-week range DKK 1,512–2,257; market value about DKK 132 billion, roughly $20.5 billion at about 6.43 kroner to the dollar). Genmab also has an American depositary receipt on Nasdaq under GMAB, where ten receipts represent one Copenhagen share; every per-share figure below is a Copenhagen share unless stated.

**Transcripts reviewed:** 8 May 2025, 7 August 2025, 8 November 2025, 17 February 2026, 14 May 2026, and the 6 August 2026 half-year call (pulled separately, since the bundled file stopped at May).

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells has changed shape twice in six quarters, and both changes were substantive rather than cosmetic.

**Phase one (May 2025 – November 2025): "we are becoming a fully owned business."** The opening framing was almost entirely about escaping dependence on partners. Jan van de Winkel opened the May 2025 call with the ambition of "becoming a fully integrated biotech independently developing and commercializing wholly owned antibody differentiated therapies," and the proof points were commercial rather than scientific: Tivdak approvals in Europe and Japan would be "the first time that Genmab will lead commercialization efforts on our own without a partner." Three named assets carried the future — epcoritamab (sold as EPKINLY and, in Europe, TEPKINLY), Rina-S, and acasunlimab — against a stated combined market opportunity of "$6 billion-plus."

**Phase two (November 2025 – today): "we bought the third leg."** In November 2025 the company announced the acquisition of Merus and its lead asset petosemtamab. That is when acasunlimab quietly left the headline trio. Compare the framing: in May 2025 the three priority programs were "epcoritamab, Rina-S and acasunlimab"; by February 2026 the three were "EPKINLY, Rina-S and petosemtamab," with acasunlimab demoted to a melanoma Phase 2 mention and then dropped from the top-line story entirely. In the same window GEN1042, the CD40/4-1BB antibody partnered with BioNTech, was killed outright — management said the head-and-neck data "did not meet our high bar for continued development" (November 2025). Both are honest portfolio pruning, but both were assets sold to investors as growth drivers before they were removed, and the substitute cost roughly $8 billion funded with $5.5 billion of new debt.

**Phase three (2026): "the year the pipeline pays."** From February 2026 the entire narrative compresses into a readout calendar. "2026 will be a defining year for all three of these programs," with "up to six potentially registrational data readouts." By the May 2026 call that had firmed — Rina-S enrolment in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer finished ahead of plan, pulling a pivotal readout forward into 2026. By August 2026 it had firmed again into named quarters. That is the arc: from a partner-independence story, through an acquisition, to a dated event calendar.

**What was quietly dropped or reframed:** acasunlimab (from headline asset to unmentioned), GEN1042 (terminated), and — most consequentially for anyone reading the screen — the reporting currency. With the 2025 accounts Genmab switched its reporting currency from Danish kroner to US dollars. That single presentational change is why the automated screen shows revenue down 82% year over year and earnings per share down 87%: DKK 21.53 billion of 2024 revenue is being compared with $3.86 billion of 2025 revenue. Underneath, 2025 revenue grew 19%. This is the single most important thing to understand about this name, and it is a measurement artifact, not a business event.

---

## 2. CLAIMS versus FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Where said | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Our total revenue grew by 19%" (full-year 2025) | 17 Feb 2026 | Reported 2025 revenue $3.86 billion versus a 2024 base that was reported in kroner. Quarterly dollar figures confirm growth, not collapse: Q1 2025 $746m → Q1 2026 $896m. | **Supported.** The screen's "−82%" is a currency-of-reporting artifact. |
| "We grew total revenue by 25%" (first half 2026) | 6 Aug 2026 | First-half 2026 revenue of about $2.05 billion against about $1.67 billion — roughly 23% on the quarterly filings, 25% on the company's own basis. | **Supported.** |
| Darzalex remains the engine but the base is diversifying | 6 Aug 2026 | Darzalex royalties up 21% in the half; EPKINLY worldwide net sales up 48%; the rest of the portfolio up 35%. Roughly half of the growth came from outside Darzalex. | **Supported and improving**, but Darzalex still supplies roughly three-quarters of revenue. |
| Own-brand commercial execution is working | 6 Aug 2026 | EPKINLY $312m and Tivdak $84m in the half — $396m of proprietary sales, up 37%. Against 2025's full-year $632m, the ramp is real. | **Supported.** |
| "We grew operating profit by 62% / 56% / 52%" while investing | 2025 calls | Operating income by quarter: Q3 2025 $459m, Q4 2025 $245m, Q1 2026 $221m, Q2 2026 $407m. Lumpy, and Q1 2026 was weak. | **Directionally supported, but the phrasing flatters.** Operating profit is not a smooth compounding line. |
| "Multibillion-dollar" peak sales for petosemtamab | 17 Feb 2026 | Anthony Pagano refused to put a number on it — "we're going to remain with our guidance in terms of multibillion blockbuster potential." Rina-S carries a specific ">$2 billion"; EPKINLY ">$3 billion". | **Unquantified.** The most expensive asset on the balance sheet is the only one without a numeric peak-sales estimate. |
| Leverage discipline: "below 3x gross leverage by the end of 2027" | 17 Feb 2026 | Net debt at 30 June 2026 is $3.77 billion including capitalised leases ($3.63 billion excluding them) against trailing twelve-month earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) of $1.39 billion — 2.7x net. Weighted effective interest rate about 6.6% on $5.5 billion raised, of which $4.1 billion is fixed after hedging. | **On track, but the interest bill is now real** — $110m per quarter, which is why first-quarter 2026 net income was only $53m. |

**The two divergences that matter.**

First, **returns have been diluted, not earned down.** Return on invested capital is 9.9% on a trailing basis against the 12.6% the screen carries and materially higher levels historically; return on equity is 13.6% against 17.1%. The cause is visible on the balance sheet: intangible assets are now 73.7% of total assets, almost entirely Merus goodwill and in-process research. The operating business did not deteriorate — gross margin in the second quarter of 2026 was 92.7% and the operating margin 35%. The denominator grew by $8 billion of acquisition. That is an important distinction: it is capital deployed, not capital destroyed, but it will only be earned back if petosemtamab works.

Second, **the reported tax rate is temporarily fictional.** The first-half 2026 effective tax rate was 3.6% — $13 million of tax expense — because Merus deferred tax assets are being recognised and used. Management said plainly it "will normalize over the next 12 to 18 months." Any earnings-per-share model built off current after-tax profitability is borrowing from a one-off.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising, and unusually specific for a biotech.**

- *May 2025* — confident but hedged on timing. On competitor questions, deliberate restraint: "it's not really appropriate for us to speculate on why or why not the FDA has asked for an ODAC."
- *August 2025* — the tone steps up sharply on hard data. The Phase 3 EPCORE FL-1 result was described as "unprecedented," with "a hazard ratio of 0.21." That is a number, not an adjective, and it was delivered on the call.
- *November 2025* — offensive language returns with the Merus deal: "a potentially transformative proposed acquisition." In the same breath, discipline on the other side of the ledger — GEN1042 terminated.
- *February 2026* — the most confident call in the set, and also the one carrying the worst single piece of news. Management led with "up to six potentially registrational data readouts" and buried the EPCORE DLBCL-1 result — progression-free survival improved, but "overall survival did not reach statistical significance."
- *May 2026* — operational confidence: enrolment finished early, "this important milestone brings forward the pivotal Phase III data."
- *August 2026* — the most precise the company has ever been. Guidance raised, and the readout calendar named to the quarter rather than the half.

**Shift in posture:** from investment-and-build language in 2025 to delivery-and-proof language in 2026. There is no defensive drift — no margin-protection or cost-programme vocabulary anywhere in six calls. If anything the risk runs the other way: management is spending into the readouts, adding two new Phase 3 colorectal studies for petosemtamab in August 2026 while raising the operating-expense guide only 2%.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High — with one disclosure blemish.**

The traceable record is good. In February 2025 management committed to three things: accelerate the late-stage pipeline, maximise the commercial medicines, and hold to capital-allocation priorities. By February 2026 all three were demonstrably delivered — the second-line follicular lymphoma approval landed, three Rina-S Phase 3 trials were running, and the Merus deal closed early in the first quarter of 2026 as promised in November 2025.

On numbers, the pattern is conservative-then-raise, which is the healthy direction. Full-year 2026 revenue guidance moved from about 14% growth to a range of $4.3–4.5 billion, roughly 19% growth at the midpoint, with the $195 million midpoint increase split about evenly between Darzalex and EPKINLY. Operating profit guidance is $1.1–1.4 billion and operating expenses $2.88 billion at the midpoint. The screen's earnings-beat rate of five of seven quarters (71%) is consistent with modest sandbagging rather than aggressive framing.

On timelines, the record is genuinely better than the industry norm. Management pulled the Rina-S platinum-resistant ovarian readout *forward* (May 2026) because recruitment ran ahead. Tahi Ahmadi has been consistently dismissive of external timeline sources — "I wouldn't take clinicaltrials.gov as the most validated resource" (May 2025) — and has so far been vindicated.

**The blemish.** On 23 July 2026, Genmab and AbbVie issued a joint release titled a "clarification on the primary endpoints" of the Phase 3 EPCORE DLBCL-1 trial, six months after the January 2026 top-line. The substance of that clarification could not be verified from the sources available for this review (the publisher blocked retrieval), so nothing is asserted here about what changed. What can be said is that a company needing to restate which endpoints were primary, half a year after announcing the result, is a disclosure-quality event and should be treated as an open item rather than a closed one. It sits alongside the earlier admission that overall survival in that trial "did not reach statistical significance," which management attributed to "COVID-19 and the increasing availability of novel anti-lymphoma therapies" — a plausible explanation that is also the standard explanation offered when a survival endpoint misses.

**Reliability score: High**, with the DLBCL-1 endpoint disclosure flagged as unresolved.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three questions come back call after call, and the quality of the answers has been uneven.

**One — "when exactly does it read out?"** Asked in some form on every call in the set. Answers ranged from a one-word deflection ("Nothing has changed," November 2025) to open irritation in August 2026, when Tahi Ahmadi responded to a multi-part timing question with "I stopped counting at 3, but okay," and Jan van de Winkel closed a follow-up with "We are not going to address any further timing and time line issues here." The company has since given the dates, so the deflection did not conceal bad news — but the reflex to shut the question down is worth noting.

**Two — "what hazard ratio do you need?"** Kalpit Patel of Wolfe Research (May 2026) and others pressed repeatedly on the bar for the frontline diffuse large B-cell trial against the competing POLARIX benchmark. Management consistently refused: "it doesn't make much sense to speculate." Reasonable, but it means investors go into a Q4 readout with no company-stated definition of success.

**Three — the competitive bar, which is rising in real time.** On the August 2026 call an analyst noted that Merck has reported hitting both progression-free and overall survival at the interim of its Trop-2 antibody-drug conjugate trial in endometrial cancer, and asked directly whether that sets the bar for Rina-S. Genmab's answer leaned on the breadth of folate-receptor-alpha expression rather than on a head-to-head comparison. Separately, James Gordon of Barclays asked the sharpest question of the set: if the frontline EPKINLY interim fails, "will you tell us that... or is it just we will not hear anything?" That is an analyst pricing in the possibility of silence.

**What analysts are not pressing on, and should be:** the Darzalex royalty duration. Across six calls, no analyst in these transcripts asked directly when the Darzalex royalty stream ends. The only patent question in the set was about EPKINLY, answered in August 2026 with a deliberately vague "mid thirties is where we are" and an explicit refusal to go further: "discussing patent and IP strategy on a call like this in the nuanced details is probably not appropriate." Three-quarters of revenue rests on an asset whose expiry the company will not discuss and analysts do not ask about.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The reporting-currency switch made the financial history unreadable.** Not deceptive — companies change presentation currency for legitimate reasons — but it produces a headline that looks like an operating collapse, and it is the reason this name reached a deep-value screen at all. Anyone using screened growth rates on this company between 2025 and 2026 is reading a rounding convention.

🔴 **Two headline assets were removed after being sold as growth drivers.** Acasunlimab and GEN1042 (November 2025).

🔴 **The endpoint clarification on EPCORE DLBCL-1** (23 July 2026), six months after the top-line — unresolved.

🔴 **Concentration remains extreme.** Darzalex royalties are roughly three-quarters of revenue, at essentially 100% margin, on an asset Genmab does not control and does not discuss the duration of.

🔴 **The balance sheet changed character.** From roughly $3 billion of net cash (August 2025: "we ended the first half with around $3 billion in cash") to $3.77 billion of net debt at 30 June 2026 — a swing of nearly $7 billion in a year, at about 6.6% blended cost. Roughly $1.4 billion of it floats unhedged.

🟢 **The commercial franchise is genuinely working.** EPKINLY up 48% in the half, Tivdak up, four launches executed in 2025 across the US, Japan and Europe, and the first two Genmab-led launches without a partner delivered as promised.

🟢 **Hard clinical wins keep landing.** EPCORE FL-1 hit both primary endpoints with a hazard ratio of 0.21 (August 2025). EPCORE DLBCL-4 met its primary endpoint on progression-free survival (29 June 2026). The European Commission approved TEPKINLY plus lenalidomide and rituximab in second-line follicular lymphoma (6 July 2026). The March 2026 label change removing the 24-hour hospitalisation recommendation is a quiet but real commercial unlock in the community setting.

🟢 **Timelines pulled forward, not pushed back** — the Rina-S ovarian readout (May 2026) is the cleanest evidence of execution in the whole file.

🟢 **Guidance raised on operating leverage, not on cost cuts** (August 2026): 5% more revenue, 7% more operating profit, 2% more spending.

🟢 **They killed a programme rather than nurse it** (GEN1042, November 2025). Capital discipline you can see.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**"Recurring revenue" is doing quiet work.** Through 2025 management repeatedly attributed growth to "increased recurring revenue" — a phrase that describes royalties. By August 2026 the framing had shifted to "high growth and broad-based growth," with the explicit point that "approximately half of our year over year revenue growth came from DARZALEX. Impressively, the other half generated by EPKINLY and the remainder of our portfolio." That is management pre-emptively building the argument that the business is less Darzalex-dependent than it looks — which tells you they know that is the question.

**"Best-in-class" has become the house adjective.** Applied to Rina-S, to petosemtamab, and to EPKINLY across every call. When a term is applied to everything it stops carrying information.

**The petosemtamab peak-sales number is conspicuously absent.** Genmab quantifies EPKINLY (">$3 billion") and Rina-S (">$2 billion") but will not quantify the asset it paid roughly $8 billion for. Anthony Pagano in February 2026: "I'm not going to front run this... in terms of guiding to when we're going to potentially update guidance."

**Two new colorectal Phase 3 trials before the head-and-neck readout** (August 2026). Management is committing capital to expand petosemtamab into a second tumour type *before* the registrational data in the first tumour type has read out. That is either high internal confidence or an expensive way to signal it. Note that the same call also disclosed the second-line head-and-neck readout slipping to the first quarter of 2027.

**Interest expense is now a visible line.** Quarterly interest expense went from $3–9 million in 2025 to $110 million in both quarters of 2026. It is the single biggest reason reported earnings per share look weak.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT

**Classification: STRENGTHENING.**

Revenue is growing at 19–25%, the guidance direction is up, the owned commercial portfolio is compounding at 37–48%, three registrational readouts arrive inside one quarter, and the balance sheet — while now levered — services itself comfortably out of $870 million of trailing free cash flow against $1.1–1.4 billion of guided operating profit. Management said what it would do in February 2025 and had done all of it by February 2026.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing:** this is not a cheap stock that happens to have catalysts. It is a fairly-valued royalty annuity with a finite life, stapled to three binary clinical bets that all resolve in the next two quarters, bought partly with $5.5 billion of borrowed money at 6.6%. The screen's "deep value" label is an artifact of the currency switch. The real question is not whether the business is good — it is — but whether roughly three-quarters of revenue running off an asset the company will not discuss the expiry of is adequately compensated at 17x enterprise value to EBITDA and 26x trailing earnings, when Regeneron trades at about 15x with net cash. Size for a binary quarter, not for a value convergence.

**Economic moat.** The moat type is **intangible and regulatory-licence** — patent-protected antibody franchises plus the DuoBody and HexaBody platforms that generate them. It is real: 92.7% gross margins and a 35% operating margin in the second quarter of 2026 do not happen without genuine protection. But it is **narrow**, because it has a stated expiry. Management's only concrete statement on patent life in six calls was "mid thirties" for EPKINLY (August 2026), and the Darzalex royalty duration — the larger question — was never addressed. The returns evidence supports narrow rather than wide: return on invested capital of 9.9% and return on equity of 13.6% are respectable but not fortress-level, and both are lower than a year ago because of the acquisition.

**Moat trend: stable.** The franchise is diversifying away from single-asset dependence (half of growth now comes from outside Darzalex, versus almost none three years ago), which is genuinely moat-building. Against that, returns on capital have been diluted by $8 billion of acquired intangibles that have not yet earned anything. Those roughly cancel. It is not widening yet; it will widen if petosemtamab and Rina-S land, and erode if they do not.

**Secular threat: manageable.** None of the structural forces that permanently impair terminal value applies here. Artificial intelligence is a research accelerant for antibody discovery, not a displacement risk. Drug-pricing pressure and Medicare negotiation are real headwinds on a large oncology franchise, but they compress price, they do not remove the need for the medicine. What Genmab faces is the ordinary pharmaceutical lifecycle — patent expiry followed by biosimilar entry — which is a dated, modellable event, not a melting base. The cheapness on the screen is a **measurement artifact**, not a fear-print and not a value trap; on a corrected reading the stock is close to fairly valued rather than cheap.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory improving · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

bull_thesis:
Start by throwing away the label our own screen attached to this company. The screen reads revenue down 82% year over year and calls Genmab a deep-value stock. Both are wrong, and for the same reason: Genmab changed its reporting currency from Danish kroner to US dollars with the 2025 accounts. Revenue of 21.53 billion kroner in 2024 became $3.86 billion in 2025, and dividing the second by the first gives exactly the minus 82% the screen prints. The screen compared kroner with dollars. The business actually grew 19% that year, grew 25% in the first half of 2026, and had its full-year outlook raised on 6 August 2026. Trailing revenue to 30 June 2026 is $4.13 billion. Nothing collapsed.

What is actually here is a company with an unusually good record of doing what it said it would do, holding three late-stage medicines that all read out inside the next four to nine months. The delivery record is the load-bearing part of the bull case, because everything else depends on trusting a timetable. Genmab started the endometrial cancer Phase 3 by the end of 2025 as promised; presented ovarian data in the first half of 2025 as promised; killed its own GEN1042 programme in the second half of 2025 exactly when it said it would decide; met the 30 November 2025 regulatory decision date in follicular lymphoma; and, most tellingly, kept finishing enrolment early. The follicular and frontline lymphoma trials accrued, in management's words on the May 2025 call, significantly faster than initially projected, and the ovarian Phase 3 completed enrolment ahead of plan, pulling its data into 2026 (May 2026 call). Timelines that move earlier are rarer and more informative than timelines that slip.

The clinical evidence so far is strong, not promissory. The EPCORE FL-1 trial in second-line follicular lymphoma cut the risk of disease worsening or death by 79% and hit both of its goals (August 2025). That result has since become an approved product in the United States and, on 6 July 2026, in Europe. The EPCORE DLBCL-4 trial in relapsed large B-cell lymphoma hit its primary goal on 29 June 2026 with another chemotherapy-free combination. In March 2026 the US regulator removed the recommendation for 24-hour hospitalisation after the first full dose of EPKINLY, which directly widens use in community clinics where most patients are actually treated. Proprietary sales grew 43% in the first quarter of 2026 to $176 million, after growing 54% across 2025 to $632 million.

The two purchased assets are where the upside lives. Rina-S, an antibody-drug conjugate targeting folate receptor alpha, produced a 55.6% confirmed response rate in heavily pretreated ovarian cancer and 50% in endometrial cancer, against roughly 15% for standard chemotherapy, with no eye toxicity, no lung inflammation and no nerve damage seen across the programme, and responses that keep running past the point where the median duration would normally be reached. It carries a breakthrough designation. Critically, it works across the whole range of folate receptor expression, which is what lets it address perhaps three times the patient population of approved competitors that require high expression. Petosemtamab, acquired with Merus, produced a 63% response rate in first-line head and neck cancer against 19% for the standard of care, carries two breakthrough designations, and is now expanding into colorectal cancer with two new Phase 3 trials announced in August 2026.

The financial case rests on a royalty annuity that the market treats as furniture. Roughly seventy per cent of revenue is a royalty on daratumumab, sold by Johnson and Johnson as DARZALEX, which did $4,207 million of net sales in the second quarter of 2026 alone. That royalty carries essentially no cost, which is why a company with a 32% operating margin on $4.13 billion of revenue throws off $870 million of free cash flow. If the three late-stage assets land, that annuity funds the transition rather than defining the company.

What has to hold: the petosemtamab first-line head and neck Phase 3 must reproduce something close to its Phase 2 response rate in a randomised setting; Rina-S must convert its response rates into an approvable result in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer; the frontline lymphoma trial must deliver; and daratumumab must hold its sales trajectory through roughly 2029 without an early price cut from government negotiation.
bear_thesis:
Genmab borrowed $5.5 billion to buy a future it has not yet proven, and the proof arrives in four months.

Start with the balance sheet, because it is the fact the earnings calls narrate least. On 30 September 2025 Genmab held $3.41 billion of cash and investments against $142 million of lease obligations: net cash of $1.62 billion. On 30 June 2026 it holds $1.50 billion of cash against $5.27 billion of borrowings: net debt of $3.77 billion. That is a $5.4 billion swing in three quarters, and it bought one asset. Against that, intangible assets on the balance sheet stand at $8.87 billion versus total shareholders' equity of $5.96 billion. The accounting value of two drugs that have never been approved exceeds the entire book value of the company. A failed Phase 3 on petosemtamab is therefore not a pipeline disappointment; it is a write-down that could erase a large fraction of book equity.

The interest bill is not fully in the numbers yet. Trailing interest expense is $269 million on $5.27 billion of debt, an effective 5.1%, because the borrowings were outstanding for only part of the period. Management stated the weighted average effective rate is around 6.6%, which annualises to roughly $350 million. Somewhere between $80 and $100 million of additional interest has still to land, against consensus 2026 operating profit of about $1.18 billion. It arrives whether or not the trials work. Management also committed to getting gross leverage below three times by the end of 2027; gross debt of $5.27 billion against consensus 2026 earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of roughly $1.25 billion is 4.2 times today. Meeting that promise on the 2027 consensus requires roughly $600 million of debt repayment out of roughly $900 million to $1 billion of free cash flow, while funding five or more Phase 3 programmes. The share buyback completed in June 2025 has no successor, and will not have one soon.

Now the thing nobody in eight quarters of earnings calls asked about. Not one analyst question in this entire file concerns what happens to the daratumumab royalty when the drug loses exclusivity. Roughly seventy per cent of Genmab's revenue, and effectively more than one hundred per cent of its profit, is a royalty on a product Genmab does not sell, protected by patents that begin to lapse around the end of this decade. Every dollar of that royalty is pure margin, so the loss is not gradual and it is not cushioned. Worse, government price negotiation on high-spend medicines can cut the royalty base years before the patents expire, pulling the cliff forward. The market's own forecasts already embed this: consensus revenue goes $5.24 billion in 2027, $6.31 billion in 2028, $6.49 billion in 2029 and $6.70 billion in 2030, and earnings per depositary receipt go $2.62, then $2.55, then $2.60 across those last three years. Flat. The street is modelling the new drugs roughly cancelling the old royalty, not adding to it.

The clinical bridge is thinner than the presentation suggests. Management's own argument for petosemtamab is that Phase 3 trials have in the past tended to mimic Phase 2 data closely. That assumption was punctured in January 2026, when the EPCORE DLBCL-1 monotherapy Phase 3 improved the time patients lived without disease worsening but failed to show a statistically significant survival benefit. Management's immediate response was to name exculpatory factors, including COVID-19 and the increasing availability of novel anti-lymphoma therapies, and the company then had to issue a formal clarification of that trial's primary goals on 23 July 2026, seven months later. Petosemtamab's headline 63% response rate is a single-arm Phase 2 number in a disease where response rate and survival have diverged before. The same bridge, the same risk.

Finally, there is no cushion in the price. At 2,261 kroner the shares sit 1.2% below a 52-week high of 2,288 and 20% above their 200-day average, having risen roughly 50% from a 52-week low of 1,512. On consensus, that is about 29 times this year's earnings and 20 times next year's. The insider buying ratio across the scan window is zero. A single missed readout takes the shares back to the 200-day average, around 1,888, without the thesis breaking at all.

What would confirm the bear case: the petosemtamab first-line head and neck Phase 3 missing or landing far below its Phase 2 response rate; a Rina-S ovarian result whose responses do not last; the frontline lymphoma trial producing a modest hazard ratio; or daratumumab being named for government price negotiation.
consensus_delta:
The market is not looking the wrong way on this stock. It is refusing to look at all at the part that matters most, and it has parked a flat line straight through the widest fork in the company's history.

Here is the tell, straight from the consensus estimates. Analysts model revenue of $5.24 billion in 2027, $6.31 billion in 2028, $6.49 billion in 2029 and $6.70 billion in 2030. Growth goes from about 20% to about 3% to about 3%. Earnings per depositary receipt go $2.62, then $2.55, then $2.60. Flat for three straight years, at a company with three late-stage medicines launching into that exact window. There is only one way to build that curve: you assume the daratumumab royalty starts eroding around 2029 and that EPKINLY, Rina-S and petosemtamab together do little more than fill the hole. The street is not bullish and it is not bearish. It has assumed a stand-off.

That assumption can be wrong in both directions, and both errors are large.

If it is too pessimistic: six potentially registrational readouts land between now and the middle of 2027. Only nine or ten analysts carry a 2030 revenue estimate at all, against eighteen for 2028, so the far years are thinly modelled and mechanically anchored. If petosemtamab reproduces anything close to its 63% first-line response rate and Rina-S converts its 50 to 56% response rates into approvals, the 2029 and 2030 line is far too flat and the shares are worth substantially more than our base case.

If it is too optimistic: the royalty is roughly seventy per cent of revenue and carries essentially no cost, so it is effectively more than one hundred per cent of profit. Government price negotiation on high-spend medicines could cut the royalty base years before the patents lapse. In that world the plateau becomes a decline, and the thirteen times earnings that 2028 appears to offer is a peak-earnings illusion rather than a cheap multiple.

The specific thing nobody is asking is striking. Across eight quarters of earnings calls in front of us, with dozens of analyst questions, not one concerns what happens to the daratumumab royalty at loss of exclusivity. Every question is about hazard ratios, folate receptor expression, readout sequencing and head and neck market share. The entire analyst conversation is about the new drugs; the old one that pays for all of them is treated as furniture. That is a genuine blind spot, and it is why we insist on valuing the royalty explicitly as a declining annuity rather than capitalising it as a perpetuity.

One more disagreement, and it is with ourselves rather than the street. Our own screen labels this a deep-value stock on an 82% revenue collapse. There was no collapse; the company changed reporting currency from kroner to dollars. The market has this right and we had it wrong: the shares sit at 96% of their 52-week range because the business is growing 25%, not because anyone is asleep. When our screen and the market disagree this violently, the burden of proof is on the screen, and here the screen fails it.
forcing_function:
One event dominates, and the rest are incremental.

The re-rating event is the petosemtamab Phase 3 readout in first-line head and neck cancer, guided to the second half of 2026 on the 17 February 2026 full-year call and reconfirmed on 14 May 2026 and 6 August 2026. Genmab paid roughly $8 billion for Merus to own this asset and borrowed $5.5 billion to do it. The Phase 2 result was a 63% response rate against 19% for the standard of care. If the randomised trial substantially reproduces that, the asset is worth more than we carry it and the $8.87 billion of intangibles on the balance sheet is validated; if it does not, the same number becomes a write-down. Nothing else in this company moves the valuation as far in either direction. A second head and neck Phase 3, in the second and third-line setting, is guided to the same window.

The second forcing event is Rina-S in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer, and there are now two datasets rather than one, both in the second half of 2026. The Phase 2 potentially registrational cohort reads out, and so does the Phase 3 RAINFOL-02 trial, which completed enrolment ahead of plan; the company disclosed that acceleration on 14 May 2026 and said it brings the pivotal data into 2026 and opens the door to broader regulatory filings earlier than expected. First approval is targeted for 2027.

The third is EPCORE DLBCL-2, EPKINLY in combination with R-CHOP in previously untreated large B-cell lymphoma, guided to 2026. This is the largest addressable population in the file, roughly 70,000 patients, and management has said it will very likely be the first frontline bispecific study to report.

The only genuinely fixed date on the near calendar is the extraordinary general meeting on 7 October 2026, convened on 8 September 2026 with a shareholder letter attached. We could not verify its agenda from the sources available to us and we will not speculate about it. We note only that a special meeting called with a letter to shareholders appended is worth reading when the papers are public.

Part of the calendar has already fired since our last look and is now spent news: the EPCORE DLBCL-4 Phase 3 met its primary goal on 29 June 2026; the European Commission approved TEPKINLY plus R2 in second-line follicular lymphoma on 6 July 2026; and the company raised its full-year outlook on 6 August 2026 alongside 25% first-half revenue growth. Those results are in our numbers and in the price.

A note on how the market environment should and should not colour this. The current regime favours situations whose resolution does not depend on a single shared macro driver, and penalises theses that need interest rates to fall. Genmab qualifies well on both counts: nothing here depends on the Federal Reserve, and the three readouts are clinically and commercially independent of one another, so one failure does not mechanically imply the others. That independence is a genuine mark in Genmab's favour. It is offset by the fact that each readout is individually a single yes-or-no outcome with no fallback, and by the fact that the company's floating-rate borrowings mean rates staying higher for longer costs it real money rather than merely sentiment.

positioning_washout:
There is no mechanical washout to wait for here, and that matters for how we express the call.

The classic forced-selling trigger does not exist. Genmab pays no dividend, so there is no income-focused shareholder base that can be evicted by a dividend cut, and no pivot that reclassifies the stock out of an index sleeve. Nothing is going to force anyone out on a schedule.

What the register does show is discretionary selling by informed holders, which is weaker evidence but not nothing. Orbis Investment Management disclosed control of 3,112,476 shares on 15 June 2026, precisely 4.99% of the share capital. Five per cent is the Danish disclosure threshold. Stopping one basis point beneath it is a deliberate act by a holder managing visibility rather than building openly. Separately, Avidity Partners Management cut its holding of the US depositary receipts by 45.7% in its most recently reported filing, disclosed 1 August 2026. Both are discretionary sellers, not forced ones.

The real pressure channel here is event-driven rather than structural. A petosemtamab Phase 3 miss would hit a register largely assembled since the Merus acquisition was announced, on a company with $8.87 billion of intangibles and no valuation floor beneath them. There is nothing mechanical to catch it: no net cash, no dividend yield, no buyback bid, no deal terms.

One structural feature is worth sizing for. The shares trade in two places and two currencies, in Copenhagen as ordinary shares and on Nasdaq as depositary receipts at ten receipts to one share. Trial results are typically released to the US market, so the receipts reprice first and the Copenhagen line opens gapped the following morning. An investor holding the Copenhagen line cannot react inside the move. Size this position for a gap, not for a slide.

Finally, a small but standing source of supply: employee warrant exercises convert almost monthly, 185 shares on 16 June 2026, 24,592 on 11 August 2026 and 28,011 on 8 September 2026. Roughly a tenth of a per cent a year, immaterial to value but price-insensitive and continuous.

The practical conclusion is that waiting for a shake-out has to mean waiting for a specific event to disappoint, not waiting for a mechanical seller to appear. So we name the level rather than the seller.
moderator_conclusion:
Our recommendation is unchanged: wait for a better entry, and this time we are naming both a price and an event that would change it.

First, correct the record, because our own screen sent this name to committee for the wrong reason. The screen reads revenue down 82% and labels Genmab a deep-value stock. Genmab changed its reporting currency from Danish kroner to US dollars with the 2025 accounts; 21.53 billion kroner in 2024 became $3.86 billion in 2025, and the ratio of those two figures is exactly the minus 82.1% printed. The business grew 19% that year, grew 25% in the first half of 2026, and had its outlook raised on 6 August 2026. There is no deep value here. The shares sit at 96% of their 52-week range because the market has the facts right and our screen had them wrong. The discounted-cash-flow fair value of 8,088 kroner in the same screen is built on the same broken series and should be discarded.

What is genuinely here is a good business at a fair-to-full price on the eve of the most consequential four months in its history. We value it at 2,800 kroner a share against a market price of 2,261, a discount of about 19%. More than half of that value, $14.0 billion of $26.4 billion, is the royalty on daratumumab, a drug Genmab does not sell, on patents that begin to lapse around the end of this decade. We value that stream as a declining annuity rather than a perpetuity, which is the discipline this name most requires and which almost nobody applies: across eight quarters of earnings calls and dozens of analyst questions, not one asks what happens to that royalty at loss of exclusivity.

The reason to wait is arithmetic, not sentiment. Nineteen per cent is below the twenty per cent minimum entry discount this book demands even in the friendliest conditions, and the shape of the trade is wrong: from 2,261 we risk about 811 kroner to our adverse case of 1,450 to make about 539 to our base case of 2,800. The favourable case at 4,350 is real and large, but it is entirely contingent on readouts that have not happened. Meanwhile the shares are 1.2% below their 52-week high and 20% above their 200-day average, there is no dividend, no active buyback, and intangible assets of $8.87 billion sit on shareholders' equity of $5.96 billion. There is nothing structural beneath the price to catch it.

We are also not being paid to guess. Up to six potentially registrational readouts arrive between now and the middle of 2027, and the largest, petosemtamab in first-line head and neck cancer, underwrites the $8 billion acquisition and the $5.5 billion of borrowing that funded it. We can watch that resolve at no cost. Management's own case for it is that its Phase 3 trials have in the past tended to mimic Phase 2 data closely, which is precisely the assumption the EPCORE DLBCL-1 monotherapy trial punctured in January 2026, when survival fell short of statistical significance and the company needed a formal clarification seven months later to explain the endpoints.

None of this is a knock on management. The delivery record is the best thing in the file and it is why we score credibility at four out of five: trials started on schedule, enrolment repeatedly finishing ahead of plan, the 30 November 2025 regulatory decision met, the follicular lymphoma Phase 3 cutting the risk of progression or death by 79%, and the discipline to kill their own GEN1042 programme on the timetable they announced. The marks against them are narrow and specific: the quantified operating-profit growth figure quietly disappeared from the prepared remarks exactly when the acquisition debt arrived, they will guide peak sales for the two assets they built and not for the one they bought, and the one real clinical disappointment was met with reasons rather than a clean account.

Two things would move us to buy, and either is sufficient.
The price coming to us: 1,950 to 2,000 kroner, a fall of about 13%, which widens the discount to our base case to roughly 30% and restores a positive balance of risk and reward. That level is above the 52-week low of 1,512 and roughly at the 200-day average, so it does not require a disaster. One disappointing readout would do it.
Or the evidence coming to us: a first-line head and neck Phase 3 for petosemtamab that broadly reproduces its 63% Phase 2 response rate. That would justify carrying the asset at $9.0 billion rather than $5.5 billion, lifting our base case to roughly 3,175 kroner and making today's price a 29% discount. We would buy the confirmation rather than the anticipation, and accept paying up for it.

On the value case judged on its own, ignoring the catalyst calendar and the market environment entirely, we move up one notch to a three out of five from a two. The business is demonstrably better than when we last looked and our estimate of its worth rose faster than the share price did. But it is not a value investment. Twenty-nine times this year's earnings and twenty times next year's, with roughly seventy per cent of revenue coming from a royalty on someone else's product that expires on a known clock, is a fair price for a good company, not a cheap one. The moat is narrow but real rather than wide: returns on invested capital of 12.6% are respectable but falling, because the acquisition roughly doubled invested capital without doubling profit, and the highest-margin revenue line is the one with the expiry date. We call the trend stable rather than eroding because the replacement is visibly being built and is landing on schedule. The structural threat we take seriously is government price negotiation on high-spend medicines, which could shrink the royalty years before the patents lapse; that is material rather than fatal, and it is a risk shared with every large biopharma name in the peer set, so we treat it as a sector-wide factor and not as a Genmab-specific discount.
